astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think it's probably a combination of these things. And I would be careful about saying that we know exactly which part comes from pre-training, which part comes from post-training, or from decoding. To really answer that, you would need controlled experiments where you change one of these things and keep the others fixed.

I think it's related to our earlier discussion of dataset bias, right? These models may all produce very reasonable answers to the same question, but that doesn't mean their distributions of answers are the same. They have their own preferences, their own habits, in what they say and how they say it.

And some of those habits could be very visible, like particular words or phrases. But there could also be differences in which information they choose to include, which examples they give, how they organize an explanation. So when you rewrite something, you may change the wording quite a lot, but you still preserve some of those choices. Otherwise, you're no longer really preserving the original answer, right? That could help explain why a signature survives rewriting or translation.

So I would think of this as a broader notion of model-specific behavior. It doesn't necessarily mean the answer is bad. Two models can both give good answers and still be distinguishable. And the fact that we can distinguish them tells us there are systematic differences. Understanding exactly where those differences come from, I think that's the more difficult and interesting question. Yeah.

sol.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think it is probably a mixture of all of these things. The most obvious signatures are style—word choice, sentence structure, how the model organizes an answer—and those are strongly affected by post-training and decoding. But what surprised us is that the signal is not only superficial “slop,” because if it were, rewriting or translating the text should remove most of it. Instead, some model identity remains.

So I think the models also have different preferences about what information to select, what to omit, what concepts to connect, and how to reason or represent the content. Those choices can originate from pre-training data, architecture and training dynamics, and then be amplified by post-training. When another model rewrites the output, it changes the surface form, but it is still rewriting a particular selection and organization of ideas, so part of the original model’s fingerprint survives.

I would not say we can cleanly assign a percentage to pre-training versus post-training yet. A good controlled experiment would take the same base model through different post-training recipes, or different base models through the same post-training recipe, and then see which signatures remain. But our main message is that model outputs contain more provenance information than we normally assume, and removing a few stylistic phrases is probably not enough to erase it.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that, that's a great question, and, and it connects back to the dataset bias work we talked about earlier. Actually the, the origin of that project is literally the same experiment. We just, we, we took the "name that dataset" idea and applied it to, to model outputs instead of images. So you give the same set of prompts to several chat models, collect the responses, and train a classifier to guess which model wrote which response. And, again, the accuracy is, is shockingly high. Like well above ninety percent for, for five or so models. So, so to a classifier, these models are, are nothing like each other, even though to us they, they all kind of feel like a helpful assistant, right?

Now, what is it measuring? I, I would say the, the cheapest, most salient signal is post-training style, and a lot of it is just formatting. Markdown habits, whether you, you like bolded headers, whether you like bullet lists, how you open a response, "Certainly," versus, versus diving right in. Some characteristic word choices. That's, that's exactly the slop you are removing, I think. But the interesting part for us was, we, we tried to destroy that. We, we strip the markdown, we lowercase everything, we have another model rewrite the response, translate it to another language and back, summarize it. And the accuracy drops, but it, it stays way above chance. So there's something left after you, after you remove the surface style. It's, it's in what the model chooses to talk about, how it decomposes a problem, how long it thinks a good answer should be, what caveats it, it feels obligated to add. So I would say it's, it's style at the shallow level and, and something more like content selection at the deeper level.

But, if you ask me where it fundamentally comes from, I, I would attribute it to data again. Mostly post-training data, the, the instruction tuning and preference data, because those are, are curated very differently by each lab and, and they're relatively small so they leave a strong fingerprint. Not so much decoding, we, we checked temperature and, and it doesn't change much. and there's a, a fun consequence, which is if you fine-tune a model on synthetic data from another model, it inherits that model's idiosyncrasy, and the classifier can, can detect it. So it's, it's kind of a, a distillation detector, almost for free. which I, I think is, is a little bit, uh, uncomfortable for, for some people, but, but scientifically it's, it's a nice signal that these fingerprints really are, are coming from the training distribution and not from the architecture, not from the decoding. Yeah.

And I, I guess the, the lesson for your anti-slop direction is that, removing the, the surface tokens gets you most of the perceptual improvement, but you shouldn't expect it to make the model, um, anonymous. The, the signature is, is deeper than the word list. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, that's a very interesting question. I tend to think it's fundamentally about the data and the training recipe, especially the differences in pre-training data mixtures and post-training alignment.

Just like in our dataset bias study, where we found that different datasets have very strong, distinct signatures that allow a model to easily tell where an image came from, large language models also inherit very distinct fingerprints from the data distributions they were trained on and the specific alignment recipes they undergo. 

Even when you apply rewriting, summarization, or translation, those underlying statistical habits—the subtle choices in phrasing, vocabulary distribution, and structure—still survive because they are so deeply baked into the model during training. So while decoding strategies or specific post-training stylistic quirks definitely play a role, I think those signatures are really measuring the unique traces left by the training data curation and post-training recipes of different labs. It's kind of like a lasting fingerprint of the data that's very hard to wash away. Yeah.

Like, if it was just, "oh, this model likes to use the word 'delve'," right, once you, once you translate the text to another language and, and translate it back, that signal should be, should be gone. But it's not. So it's measuring something deeper, like, what, what concepts the model tends to bring up, how it organizes content, the, the kind of semantic-level habits of, of its outputs.

So my belief is it's, it's mostly a fingerprint of the training data, like, going back to my, my usual thesis, right? The model is kind of a reflection of what, what data it was trained on. And every lab has a different pre-training mixture, different post-training data, different annotator preferences in, in RLHF. All of these bake a very consistent distribution into the model, and that, that distribution shows up no matter what transformations you apply to the text afterwards.

I would guess decoding plays a smaller role, because, if you change the sampling temperature or, or the decoding strategy, the outputs change a lot, but the signature is still there. So it's, it's more structural than, than decoding.

And actually, we, we found a, a practical use of this, which is detecting whether one model was distilled from, from another. Because if a model is trained on the outputs of another model, it inherits a lot of that signature. So in some sense, the, the signature is really measuring the, the lineage of the model, like, what data, what teacher, what recipe it came from. Yeah.
